To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) distinct stages of the visual pathway are modulated by the familiarity of a face; and (ii) the mechanisms for processing familiar faces differ from those for processing unfamiliar faces.

Familiar faces elicit stronger early responses than unfamiliar faces in the visual cortex, but this effect is only observed in the case of upright faces, and the effect is lost in the extended face processing network.

the neural mechanisms for the processing of familiar faces differ from those for unfamiliar faces along the time domain, as revealed by the distinct spatio‐temporally patterns of activity evoked in different visual areas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of visual processing and face recognition.
the neural mechanisms that mediate face processing in humans and how these mechanisms change with the presentation frequency.
how we recognize familiar faces and the underlying neural mechanisms that support this ability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the processing of familiar faces is faster and less resource‐consuming than the processing of unfamiliar faces, and that this is due to the fact that familiar faces are processed at a higher level of visual processing, which is more efficient and requires fewer resources.
the processing of familiar faces is faster than that of unfamiliar faces, but only for early visual processing, and that familiarity processing is modulated by face orientation.

familiarity processing is modulated by both early and late visual processing stages, but the exact nature of this modulation depends on the specific frequency of the stimulus presentation and on the orientation of the faces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the neural responses to faces are modulated by familiarity in a frequency‐dependent manner, with early visual areas responding to familiar faces, but not unfamiliar faces, and higher visual areas responding to unfamiliar, but not familiar, faces.
the visual system is sensitive to face familiarity at multiple processing stages, but that the mechanisms for processing familiarity are different at each stage.
familiarity is processed differently at different levels of visual hierarchy, with early visual stages showing a preference for familiar faces, whereas higher visual areas show no preference.
The main takeaway from our work is that
different stages of the face recognition system are differentially sensitive to the familiarity of the face.
the mechanisms mediating face recognition are not uniform throughout the visual hierarchy.
the neural mechanisms underlying familiar face recognition are different from those underlying unfamiliar face recognition.
